aiTutor.recap: Chatbots can sound sure while being wrong, so anything that matters needs a second check.

glossary.definition: To confirm that something is true by checking it against a reliable, separate source.

paragraphs: Made-up story: Kemi asks a chatbot for a statistic for her school presentation. It gives a precise number and the name of a report. She puts both on her slide. Later she finds that the report does not exist.

The chatbot did not lie on purpose. It wrote text that looked like a real fact. Names, numbers, dates, quotes and web links are the things it gets wrong most easily, because they must be exactly right.
The habit is simple: use the answer as a starting point, and check the parts that matter before you rely on them or share them.

aiTutor.explain: Tap each step. You do not need all four every time, but the more it matters, the more you do.

nodes.label: 1. Spot
nodes.title: Spot the risky parts
nodes.definition: Mark the exact facts: names, numbers, dates, quotes, links and any advice with real consequences. These are the parts to check.
nodes.bonusFact: General explanations are usually safer than precise facts.

nodes.label: 2. Ask
nodes.title: Ask it to show its basis
nodes.definition: Ask "How sure are you?" or "What source is this from?". The answer is a clue, not proof, because it can invent sources too.
nodes.bonusFact: A source you cannot find yourself is a warning sign.

nodes.label: 3. Cross-check
nodes.title: Cross-check elsewhere
nodes.definition: Look the fact up in a separate, reliable place: an official website, a trusted news outlet, a textbook, or an expert. Two independent sources that agree are better than one.
nodes.bonusFact: Do not use the same chatbot to confirm its own answer.

nodes.label: 4. Decide
nodes.title: Decide what to use
nodes.definition: Keep what you confirmed, fix what is wrong, and leave out anything you could not check. For health, law or money, also ask a qualified person.
nodes.bonusFact: Leaving out an unchecked fact is better than sharing a wrong one.

widgetData.completionMessage: You have the four steps: spot, ask, cross-check, decide.
widgetData.completionBonusFact: The more a mistake would cost, the more steps you should take.

aiTutor.explain: Look for the exact, checkable fact.

widgetData.question: A chatbot writes a paragraph about a famous event. Which part should you check first?
widgetData.explanation: Exact facts are where a polished-looking answer is most often wrong, and where a mistake does the most damage.
widgetData.bonusFact: A quick search for one key name or number often reveals whether the whole answer is solid.

aiTutor.explain: Decide whether each statement is true or false.

widgetData.instruction: Is each statement true or false?

cards.statement: A source or web link given by a chatbot is real because it looks proper.
cards.explanation: Chatbots can invent sources and links. Open the link, or search for the source yourself.
cards.bonusFact: Search for the source's name yourself. If you cannot find it, do not use it.

cards.statement: Asking the same chatbot "Are you sure?" is a full check.
cards.explanation: It may repeat or change its answer without checking anything. Use a separate source.
cards.bonusFact: Use a different, reliable place for the check, not the chatbot that wrote the answer.

cards.statement: For health, law or money decisions, a chatbot answer should be checked with a qualified person.
cards.explanation: A wrong answer here can cost you a lot, so it is worth a second, expert opinion.
cards.bonusFact: A pharmacist, doctor, lawyer or adviser can confirm what a chatbot may only have guessed.

cards.statement: If two independent trusted sources agree with the answer, you can feel more confident.
cards.explanation: Independent agreement is the best everyday check you have.
cards.bonusFact: Two sources that found their facts separately and agree are much stronger than one.
